title: Wildlife Crossing
excerpt: The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing will open on December 2. It goes over a 10-lane section of U.S. 101 in Los Angeles County, California. That’s one of the country’s busiest highways.
content:
The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing will open on December 2. It goes over a 10-lane section of U.S. 101 in Los Angeles County, California. That’s one of the country’s busiest highways. Construction of the bridge began more than four years ago. The $114 million project is now nearly complete.

Once finished, the new wildlife bridge will be the largest ever built. Coyotes, foxes, and other animals will safely make their way across.

A Freeway in the Way

Freeways are a problem for wild animals. They split habitats. Then animals can’t safely go from one side to the other. “Without a safe and sustainable wildlife crossing, movement between these remaining areas of natural habitat is severely restricted,” reads a statement on the state of California’s website. “Wildlife within the Santa Monica Mountains is essentially trapped.”

Jeff Sikich is a wildlife biologist. He works for the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. He leads a mountain lion study there. Sikich told TIME for Kids that the 101 freeway “is a major barrier” for the lions. It separates those living there from those farther to the north.

When animal groups remain apart for a long time, they encounter problems. For example, Sikich says, the mountain lions “have fewer opportunities to find mates from other areas.” The entire population gets weaker. The new wildlife crossing will give them, and other species, a path forward.

For All Animals

Seth Riley is another biologist for the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. He leads the wildlife team. Riley says the crossing was created for all sizes of animals. “Some of the smallest animals may do more than cross it,” he told TFK. “Lizards, insects, and small mammals might even make their homes on or near the crossing as the native plants grow.”

Freeways are busy. They’re noisy. Animals are scared away. But the crossing is covered with soil and plants. Small rock piles provide hiding places. When the bridge is finished, it will look and feel like a natural part of the land.

Scientists will use remote cameras and tracking collars to see what animals show up. More than 50 cameras will watch the crossing and the land around it. Riley remembers a small fence lizard. It climbed to the top of the crossing while it was being built. The bridge wasn’t connected to either side yet. But the lizard was already investigating. “Wildlife is often more curious and adaptable than we expect,” Riley says.

Beth Pratt works for the National Wildlife Federation. She helped lead the campaign to build the crossing. As Pratt told the Los Angeles Times in January, “Build it, and they really do come.” Remembering P-22 P-22 was a famous mountain lion. He lived in Griffith Park. That’s in the middle of Los Angeles. For a decade, scientists tracked and studied him. He died in 2022. People gathered for a memorial (above) in his honor in 2023.

Jeff Sikich has called P-22 an “important ambassador for urban wildlife.” P-22 showed how a big cat might manage to live in a busy city, despite the many challenges. The new wildlife crossing is part of his legacy.

title: Practice Mission
excerpt: Do you have what it takes to go to Mars? Or, at least, to pretend to go to Mars? NASA is seeking four participants for a yearlong simulated mission to space.
content:
Do you have what it takes to go to Mars? Or, at least, to pretend to go to Mars? NASA is seeking four participants for a yearlong simulated mission to space. The Moon and Mars Exploration Analog might start as early as August 2027.

The participants won’t actually go to space. According to a NASA press release, this mission will simulate “multiple parts of a moon or Mars mission.” It will help NASA understand what astronauts might go through during deep-space travel or while living on Mars. No one has ever been to Mars, so the dangers aren’t fully known. This analog is a safe test run.

Life on “Mars”

Recruits will go to the Johnson Space Center, in Houston, Texas. They’ll live in two facilities. One looks like the interior of a spacecraft. The other is modeled after a Mars habitat.

The four participants will live in the facilities for a year. They’ll go on virtual spacewalks and deal with communication delays, and be away from family and friends.

Sara Whiting is a scientist for NASA’s Human Research Program. She spoke with TFK about how this mission will serve future space travel. “We want to develop permanent habitation on the moon, and learn how to do that really well,” Whiting says. “We can then take that and translate it to Mars.”

Before that can happen, NASA needs information. On a real Mars mission, for example, it would be hard for NASA to send help or supplies in an emergency. The simulation will give NASA data to help astronauts “be healthy, be happy, and be successful” on future missions, Whiting says.

title: Insects once had 24 legs
excerpt: A many-legged creature from long ago helps fill a major gap in the fossil record — and hints at how today’s insects ended up with just six legs.
content:
Insects are famous for their six-legged bodies. But that wasn’t always the rule. A 324-million-year-old fossil dug up in west Texas had a different setup. This ancient curiosity sported a whopping 18 extra legs along its belly. That’s a body plan unlike any of today’s insects.

It is one of the oddest insects ever found, the researchers say. They reported their findings August 26 in the journal Nature.

This discovery “straddles a big gap in the fossil record,” says Erik Tihelka. As a paleoentomologist, he uses fossils to study prehistoric insects. He works at the University of Cambridge in England.

Explainer: Insects, arachnids and other arthropods

The ancient fossil sheds light on the evolution of today’s insects from their many-legged, shrimplike ancestors, Tihelka says. “It shows that there were these transitional forms along the way” — before insects settled on six legs.

Tihelka and his team called the fossil Chosha praecursor. This name was inspired by the Navajo creation myth in which the world was inhabited by insect-like people. In that myth, their descendants would go on to spread across the Earth. The fossil’s name combines the Navajo word for “insect” (ch’osh) with the Latin for “predecessor.”

A case of mistaken identity

The fossil had started out with a very different name. It was collected in 1985 from a rocky outcrop near Big Bend National Park. That’s in southwestern Texas. At first, scientists thought it was a juvenile (young) crustacean called Tesnusocaris goldichi. Other examples of this animal had already been found in the same kinds of rocks. Researchers saw little importance in the find and for years tucked it away in a museum drawer in San Diego.

Then Tihelka spotted a drawing of the fossil in a Russian paleontology book that he had bought secondhand. He tracked down the original research on it. But he had a funny feeling about this specimen having being classed as a crustacean. So he traveled to the San Diego Museum of Natural History to see it for himself.

At first glance, the fossil simply looked like a “black smudge,” Tihelka recalls. Then he looked at it again through polarized light filters. These cut reflections and sharpened the image. Now, he could make out new details. And these suggested the fossil was an early insect.

Tihelka saw a middle section, or thorax. It was divided into three segments — just like insects today. He also saw a long abdomen with 11 sections. Insects today have abdomens with seven to 11 sections.

The fossil also had a whiplike antenna on its head, a stiff tube for laying eggs and a long central tail between two shorter ones. And, of course, it had three pairs of walking legs.

There was just one small problem: The Chosha fossil didn’t just have three pairs of walking legs. Nine extra pairs of short, stubby legs emerged from its abdomen. The ones in the back were shaped like paddles. These may have helped the insect swim or scuttle through muddy shallow seas.

More such ancient, multi-legged insects?

What really surprised Tihelka was that he had seen other fossils like it.

One was a 405-million-year-old specimen from Scotland. He also recalled an undescribed pair of multi-legged, insect-like fossils from a site in Illinois.

Tihelka compared the bodies of these ancient oddballs with other insects and crustaceans, both living and extinct. Such comparisons help scientists figure out which organisms an unknown fossil is related to. And that helps them assign fossils to different groups. For instance, does its body plan resemble an insect, such as a grasshopper or ant? Or is it more like a crustacean, such as a shrimp or crab?

Placed on a family tree, Tihelka could see that Chosha and the fossils from Scotland and Illinois all landed in the same place. They all sat just outside the group that contains every insect alive today.

That makes them an ancient ancestor of today’s insects. Crustaceans were a distant branch on that family tree. They’re more of a cousin than immediate kin.

Adapting to life on land

Looking at old evidence with new tools is changing how scientists view Chosha and its many-legged relatives. With both walking and paddlelike legs, Chosha likely lived a semi-aquatic lifestyle. At some point in the millions of years since, one such early insect likely made the leap to living on land full-time.

Over many, many generations, these insect ancestors evolved to develop fewer legs. Eventually, only six remained. That land-based ancestor then gave rise to the millions of insect species on Earth today.

“It’s a funny thing,” Tihelka says. “We call insects ‘hexapods,’ meaning six legs. But it turns out that the original ones had many more.”

For all its strangeness, though, Chosha may may help clear up how insects made the jump from water to land.

“This fossil is a major milestone in a puzzling period when everything was changing from mostly aquatic to terrestrial,” says Dany Azar. He’s a paleoentomologist. He works at Lebanese University in Fanar and the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology in China. Almost no fossil evidence exists of insects from that ancient time, between roughly 325 to 400 million years ago, he notes.

William Shear is a retired paleobiologist from Hampden-Sydney College in Virginia. Chosha “opens a lot of doors to the study of insect evolution,” he says. “And one can only hope that more fossils of this particular organism will turn up upon further searching.”

title: A new flying drone uses touch to perch like a bird
excerpt: The drone's human-inspired fingers use touch to get a grip. This avoids some obstacles that come with relying on vision to perch.
content:
A new flying robot uses a deft touch to attach itself securely to a branch.

Grasping onto a landing spot could allow drones to post up in certain places for long periods of time. That way, they could monitor factories, power lines and other infrastructure — or explore remote places. But roboticists have found it hard to reliably help their drones get a grip.

Many drones have relied on vision to perch. But in crowded spaces, vision can be blocked. Then the robot may fail to attach. Sometimes, even a drone’s own grippers block its view during landing. The new robot’s design overcomes that challenge by relying not on vision but instead on touch sensors.

This drone can now feel its way onto a branch or similar landing spot. And once attached, its three human-inspired fingers need no extra energy to hold on indefinitely.

Researchers described this new design August 22 in npj Robotics.

Learning from birds

Anton Bredenbeck is a roboticist at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands. He was part of a team that wanted to build a robot that could help study vulnerable ecosystems and their species. But to do so, the drone would need to stay in those places for a while.

“The problem,” Bredenbeck says, “is that drones are really, really inefficient flyers.” Imagine scientists wanted to send a drone into a forest for a month. A drone couldn’t fly nonstop for that long. So his team took a different approach. “Let’s see how we can attach our flyers to the environment.”

Their approach was inspired by the animal world. From a distance, birds may use vision to spot a place to perch. But touch guides the final moments of their landing.

The new drone does its own version of perching by grasping onto things and hanging below. To do this, it uses three human-inspired fingers. They’re positioned like a thumb, pointer finger and middle finger. Each has three segments of different lengths. Just as in human fingers, these segments are known as phalanges (Fah-LAN-jees). The shortest segment is at a finger’s tip. The longest attaches to the robot. This makes the grasp adaptable to different shapes.

The inside of each finger has touch sensors that surround silicone pads. When the sensors touch something, the drone knows where it should move and whether to close its fingers to grasp.

The phalanges are connected by bendable joints with springs. Those springs keep the fingers in a closed position, kind of like the springs in a clothespin or a claw hair clip. Because of the springs, once the fingers have grasped onto something, they can stay in place without using any extra energy.

But the fingers do need to be opened by a motor before the robot can grip onto a perch. So they’re each connected to and controlled by a metal cord. Those cords act like the tendons in human fingers. When the motor pulls on these artificial tendons, the joints all straighten to open the fingers.

“I was really surprised how well that worked,” Bredenbeck says. The fingers adapt to many shapes without the design being too complex. “We just have a tendon. We pull on the tendon. And the finger will comply and adapt to the target.”

Engineering for the real world

“It’s a good example of embodied intelligence,” Cecilia Laschi says of the new drone. A roboticist, Laschi specializes in systems with soft parts. She works at the National University of Singapore and did not work on the new drone.

Embodied intelligence is how roboticists describe the design of certain robots and living creatures. This type of intelligence doesn’t come from a brain or computer exerting control. Instead, it comes from a design that adapts naturally to its environment.

So far, the Delft drone has only been tested in the lab. There, it does not have to search far for a spot to grasp and perch. The real world would likely present bigger challenges. Bredenbeck would like to see how much better a future drone might work if it could use both vision and touch.

Similar human-inspired fingers and hands have been designed before. But this drone lets them take flight. And it can reliably perch if a place is available within a few meters (yards). It also can grab onto a variety of things besides branches, including a traffic cone, a T-shaped piece of metal and a human arm. In each of 26 tests, the robot successfully grasped on in less than 70 seconds.

Even if this drone could see, it still wouldn’t be as adaptable as a bird, points out David Lentink. Machines designed by human engineers are just not as versatile as living things, says this scientist and engineer at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands. And he would know. Back when he was at Stanford University, he, too, developed a bird-inspired grasping drone.

Engineers often avoid developing components that are too complex, too costly or too challenging, he explains. But the natural world can still inspire new ways for solving engineering problems, Lentink says.

Indeed, this study represents an exciting direction for robotics, adds Laschi. She has noticed that new robots can be “good at running, jumping — but not as good [at] interactions with the environment. When they manipulate objects, they are not that smooth. They are not that effective,” she notes.

“Robotics is about interacting physically with things,” she says. “I think it’s what we need in robotics today.” The new drone’s design lends itself to do just that.

title: Scientists Say: Occultation
excerpt: Thanks to one of these events in 1977, astronomers discovered Uranus's rings.
content:
Occultation (noun, “uh-kuhl-TAY-shion”)

An occultation is when one celestial object passes in front of another that looks smaller in the sky. For instance, the moon or an asteroid might block the light from a distant star.

Occultations occur pretty much every night. As the moon wanders across the night sky, it passes in front of stars and planets. These are called lunar occultations.

Less common are planetary occultations. This is when a planet blocks a distant object from view. These events give astronomers a chance to learn new things about the planet, such as features of its atmosphere.

Occultations sometimes lead to discoveries. In 1977, Uranus passed in front of a distant star. Astronomers noticed the star’s light dimmed five times before Uranus completely blocked it. The star also flickered five times after the occultation.

Astronomers realized that Uranus must have rings like Saturn. Uranus’s rings do not glow brightly like Saturn’s. That made them harder to detect. But each time the star dimmed, one of Uranus’s five rings was blocking its light.

Occultations have helped scientists learn about our moon, too. Watching how starlight flickers as it passes behind the moon can reveal mountains and valleys. Timing how long stars disappear behind asteroids can help scientists measure the sizes of these space rocks.

The word occultation is similar to two other terms in astronomy: eclipse and transit. When the moon passes in front of and blocks out the sun, for example, we get a total solar eclipse.

A transit happens when one smaller-looking object passes in front of a larger one. This is what happens when an exoplanet passes in front of the distant star it’s orbiting.

title: Mystery solved? Why ‘sleeping’ ants suddenly explode with activity
excerpt: For decades, scientists have puzzled over what triggers some colonies of ants to burst from rest into community-wide action. Math may now explain this.
content:
A behavior seen among colonies of some ants has mystified scientists for more than 30 years. It’s their ability to suddenly burst into action, despite no leader telling the others when to start. What triggers this community call to action has remained a mystery — until now.

Colonies of acorn ants often spend long stretches resting quietly. It’s like everyone’s asleep. Then, points out a trio of researchers, “like a cascade of dominoes, a massive spike of activity sweeps through the nest.” It’s one example of what’s known as collective behavior. That trio — a biologist and two engineers — teamed up to explore what might serve as the alarm that tells everyone to wake up and get to work.

Since they couldn’t tap into the ants’ thinking, the researchers decided to model what they were observing. And to do this, they turned to math.

Their new computer model confirms that a single ant is all it takes to get things moving. Its motion kick-starts activity in the ants it meets, who in turn do the same to every ant they meet. But — and this is important — the model finds that the initial ant can spark activity throughout the rest of its colony only when three conditions line up.

Michael Napoli and Maurizio Porfiri are engineers at New York University in New York City. Biologist Simon Garnier works at the New Jersey Institute of Technology in Newark. They shared their new findings August 5 in PRX Life.

How one ant wakes a colony

Their model starts with a colony of quiet ants. Then, it lets any member start moving. Who it is can be quite random. As a moving ant bumps a neighbor, it sets that second ant into action. But once an ant stops moving, the model found, it would need to rest for a while before it can become active again.

Three conditions seem to limit whether an individual can spark everyone else into action. The first is how quickly activity can travel through the colony. Think of a game of tag. You tag more people if you run fast — or if the playground is packed and someone’s always within reach. Ants work the same way. Activity spreads when ants move fast enough to keep bumping into nestmates or when the nest is crowded. In a really packed nest, the first ant (and all the rest) barely need to move before others are being jostled.

Condition two is how easily ants respond to being bumped. When a moving ant reaches a still one, that neighbor has to be likely to start moving, too. If ants are hard to stir, the spark fizzles. One ant wanders the nest but wakes nobody; everyone else stays asleep.

The last condition is the trickiest. The whole colony has to switch off — go into rest mode — before the next spark. This, it turns out, is a balancing act. If ants settle down too slowly, the colony never fully settles down. But if they settle too quickly, the early motions die out before they can spread to many others.

In the model, colonies that met all three conditions burst. Those that fell short of any one of those conditions didn’t. Scientists call this kind of flip — from a colony that never bursts to one that does — a phase transition. Physicists use this term for “drastic shifts, like liquid water freezing into solid ice,” the team explains.

How well does the model match real ants?

The team built its model using measurements that others had made on real acorn ants. These included how fast they walk and how long they walk before stopping. A few features, such as the resting period, had to be estimated from the behavior of whole colonies.

Kirsten Prior expected a more biological explanation, such as a chemical signal or some form of decision-making. “Instead, this study suggests bursts come down to simply speed and contact rate,” she says. “That’s a bit humbling to me as an ant biologist.”

Prior, who works at Binghamton University in New York, studies how ants shape forests by carrying seeds around. She had no role in the new work.

“Since this paper relies on computer [models], experiments with real colonies will be necessary to test the predictions of the model,” says Grant Navid Doering. A biologist at Bilkent University in Ankara, Turkey, he studies how ant colonies coordinate their behaviors. Napoli, Garnier and Porfiri used measurements from Doering’s earlier work to set some of the numbers in their new model.

Elva Robinson wants to know what purpose the bursts serve. The model, she says, has opened a “black box” on one behavior — how bursts happen. But it does not explore what a colony gains from them. And that is of particular interest to Robinson, who tracks individual ants inside colonies. An ecologist, she works at the University of York in England.

Ants may not be the only creatures that work this way, the new study’s authors point out. They suspect the same conditions could apply anywhere individuals set each other off. Take a 2015 study of grazing sheep, for instance. There, one animal moving close to its neighbor started a chain reaction that caused the whole herd to pack tightly together. As with the ants, no one gave an order. But once action starts, it spreads to the whole group.

title: Hydrogels could help stop wildfires from reigniting, teens find
excerpt: The brothers custom built a nozzle to spray their fire-retardant hydrogels up to 60 feet.
content:
For twin brothers Jack and Henry Grover, 14, fighting wildfires is a problem close to home. They nearly lost their house to a fire. Later, they learned that the 2025 Palisades fire in their home state of California was caused by another fire that rekindled. The pair decided to see if materials called hydrogels could be sprayed onto burned areas to keep smoldering wildfires from relighting.

Hydrogels can absorb and release lots of water. Because they break down in the environment, they might be more eco-friendly than other fire retardants. Jack and Henry tested nine low-cost and widely available hydrogels. They measured how fast different ones dried out in the oven, how well they stuck to leaves and how fast they sopped up water.

The best of these was sodium polyacrylate (Pah-lee-AK-rih-layt). This super-absorbent gel is used to make diapers and sanitary napkins. It’s also known to have flame-resistant properties.

In a further test, Jack and Henry applied this gel to hot charcoal. They measured how long it took the charcoal to reignite, compared to burned charcoal sprayed with water. Water-sprayed charcoal relit in three minutes. The charcoal treated with hydrogel took nearly a half hour — about 10 times longer.

Jack and Henry did this project in eighth grade at Riverside STEM Academy in California. Their research earned them finalist spots at the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. That program is run by Society for Science, which also publishes Science News Explores. Jack and Henry both took home top prizes of $10,000 at the competition. Here, the two share their research experiences and advice.

What was your reaction to seeing your charcoal test results?

Jack and Henry were both surprised in the moment at how well the hydrogel worked. “But when we look back on it, it wasn’t entirely surprising,” Henry says. “With water, it just rolls right off or evaporates, while hydrogels hit and will stick and release that [water] over a long period of time. So much more of the water is actually used and actually cools down the rekindling material.”

What was the most challenging part?

“Testing out the hydrogel,” Jack says. “It’s not like we could waltz up to some wildfire, wait for the firefighters to put it out and then test out our product.” Instead, the pair came up with a model to represent rekindling. “We used things like the oven and the barbecue, because those are safer than testing it with a giant fire.”

What was the most rewarding part?

Jack and Henry agree that the best part of the project was 3-D printing and testing a nozzle to spray their hydrogel. “We were able to just connect it to our hose and see how far and how well it sprayed,” Henry says. The nozzle launched the gel about 18 meters (60 feet). “It was really just quite fun to see how well the device actually works,” Henry says.

Any advice for picking a science fair partner?

“You’ve got to work with somebody you know you work well with, and it’s gotta be somebody who’s actually going to help with the project,” Jack says. “Don’t just work with someone who you enjoy spending time with but is just going to goof off and not do any of the work. You’ve got to make sure you’re finding a partner who’s going to be responsible and do their work as well.”

title: Meet the first new living cat species described in more than a century
excerpt: Genetic tests on two of these teeny tiger cats, found in Bolivia, show they constitute a new species. They add a new branch to the feline family tree.
content:
Attention cat lovers: An adorable new branch has just been added to the feline family tree.

Meet Leopardus tilcayo. These pint-size “tiger cats” have a slender body, spotted fur and a ringed tail. They weigh only about two kilograms (4.4 pounds), about as much as a four-month-old domestic kitten. Discovered in Bolivia, they appear native to the Yungas forests of the central Andes Mountains.

In a paper in the October 5 Current Biology, scientists for the first time named and described L. tilcayo. Indeed, it’s the first new living cat species noted by scientists in more than a century. The last one was the Uruguayan pampas cat (L. fasciatus), first described in 1923.

For such a tiny critter, L. tilcayo has caused quite a splash. News of its new-species status pounced into headlines around the world. “I did not at all expect attention at this scale,” says Jonas Lescroart. He’s an evolutionary biologist at the University of Antwerp in Belgium.

‘House cat’ proved to be a novel species

Lescroart and his team never set out to discover a new cat. They were looking to narrow down how many tiger-cat species there are. Native to the American tropics, these tiny felines look a lot alike, Lescroart notes.

To see beyond these kitties’ coats, his team analyzed the genetics of 38 species in the Leopardus genus. This grouping includes tiger cats as well as some far-better known species, such as the ocelot. The researchers expected to find between two and possibly four distinct tiger-cat species. Instead, their new analyses point to five. One of these had never been described in the scientific record: L. tilcayo.

Data on it come from just two specimens. One is a female that was treated briefly for injuries at a sanctuary in Bolivia. (Later, it was released back into the wild.) The second, a male, still lives at the sanctuary. His name is Tigrino.

Lescroart’s colleague, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, met Tigrino at that sanctuary. She had noticed that he looked a bit different from the cats she expected to see in the area. And she has more than a little experience with such felines. She’s a cat conservationist (and National Geographic Explorer). Curious, Nogales-Ascarrunz genetically tested Tigrino. Afterward, she reached out to Lescroart’s team to share her data.

This new work suggests that there can be diversity hiding even among well-studied animals, such as cats. “I don’t know if you’ll have to wait another 100 years for a new species,” Lescroart says. Then again, his team admits it currently has no other odd kitties on its radar.

title: Is Remote Work Good for Society?
excerpt: In August, research firm Gallup released a poll. It surveyed U.S. employees who have “remote-capable jobs,” or jobs that can be done anywhere.
content:
In August, research firm Gallup released a poll. It surveyed U.S. employees who have “remote-capable jobs,” or jobs that can be done anywhere. The poll found that 25% of these employees work only remotely. There are lots of benefits to remote work—but there are also downsides. Recent research suggests that, while many people enjoy full-time remote work, it can contribute to loneliness and a decline in social skills. So: Is remote work good for society? We asked TFK readers for their thoughts on the issue. Jisu Hong, 10

Uiwang-si, South Korea Remote work is good for society because it gives people more time to live their lives. It can help people have better work-life balance. They can spend more time with their family, because they don’t have to commute to work. Remote work can help people save money on transportation and even food. People who live far from a big city might have more job opportunities with remote work. And people with disabilities or family responsibilities might find remote work more accessible. It might feel lonely sometimes, but overall, remote work can be good for society. Tigran Karapetyan, 9

Los Angeles, California Remote work is bad for society. A study published in Science in June 2026 suggests that remote workers are more isolated, anxious, and depressed than people who work in person. Another reason for my opinion is that remote work might lessen workers’ social skills. A 2024 survey conducted by Resume Builder found that one in four remote employees says working from home has led to a decline in their social skills.

People who disagree might say that working from home could save money on things like gas. To that, I say yes, but humans are social creatures.

Elizabeth Rawley, 10

Foster City, California Remote work is good for society. With remote work, you can wake up later than usual because you don’t have to worry about driving to work early in the morning. If you do wake up early, you can enjoy a nice breakfast or take a relaxing bath instead of driving to the office. Then when work starts, you will feel refreshed and ready to start your day.

With remote work, you’re not trapped inside. You can breathe fresh air. As long as you don’t slack off, remote work is good for society. You might not be working in an office, but you’re still working!

Olivia Kelly, 11

Lenox Dale, Massachusetts Remote work is not good for society. We already have AI, phones, and computers. All of these things make for less social time with friends and coworkers. Working remotely means not being face-to-face with people. It means creating a life where people think it’s okay to not see others face-to-face. This affects the way we live. This lifestyle can affect kids’ brains, too.

Remote work could be creating a bad society. This is true not only for adults, but for kids who are watching and learning. The Next Debate: Do we still need daylight saving time? title: Ask Angela: Bounce Back
excerpt: Have questions? Angela Haupt connects with experts and shares their words of wisdom. Angela Haupt is a health and wellness editor at TIME. She talks with experts about problems readers are having.
content:
Have questions? Angela Haupt connects with experts and shares their words of wisdom. Angela Haupt is a health and wellness editor at TIME. She talks with experts about problems readers are having. Then she writes articles to share what she learns. Here, she writes about what to do when you make a mistake. I said something awkward at school. I’m feeling embarrassed. How can I apologize?

We all make mistakes. Sometimes, you’re making one. Sometimes, it’s someone else. I spoke with etiquette experts to learn how you can dig yourself out of an awkward situation—and when you should take a breath and let it go. Pause and consider.

After saying something you regret, you might turn red with embarrassment. Then you might feel the urge to keep talking. People often try to defend or excuse an unfortunate remark, says Karina Schumann. She’s a psychologist. You should put aside your need to explain yourself, she says: “Think, ‘If I were on the receiving end of this, what would I need to hear?’”

Pause. Note the impact of what you said. Then take responsibility. Schumann suggests phrasing it like this: “I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have assumed.” Or: “I can see my joke wasn’t funny. I apologize.” Then take a breath. More words can come later. Match your apology to the mistake.

Call someone by the wrong name? A quick “Sorry about that!” is enough. Hurt someone’s feelings? That might call for more. An explanation can sometimes make what happened easier to understand, Schumann says. Lead with: “I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have said that.” Then ask whether an explanation would be helpful. Resist making repeated apologies.

For a minor blunder, one sincere apology is enough. “The more you apologize, the more it’s about you,” Lizzie Post says. She’s copresident of the Emily Post Institute and a great-great-granddaughter of the famous etiquette expert. The next time you meet, act normal.

When you see the person, say hi. Don’t bring up the mistake again. If you’ve apologized and the other person is ready to move on, follow their lead.

title: Scientists Say: Noise
excerpt: To analyze a messy set of data, scientists must distinguish real information from background “noise.”
content:
Noise (noun, “NOYZ”)

When talking about data, noise refers to unwanted junk data or interference. To make sense of those data, you must account for or weed out that noise.

You can think of noise like static. Listening to a radio station with a lot of static makes it harder to understand what is being said. Television static makes it hard to see what is happening. Sometimes, noise in data can make it hard to tell what’s really happening.

Noise can enter data in several ways. Very sensitive sensors may make mistakes and seem to detect things that are not really there. Or they might register a small signal as larger than it really is. People may also input wrong information into a dataset, creating noise.

Data can also become corrupted. Corruption happens when something accidentally alters some data after they’re collected. Digital data might get distorted when converted from one file type to another. Errors might also develop during storage of certain digital data. For instance, compressing and storing data in a certain format may require numbers get rounded. That rounding might introduce errors. These types of events can introduce noise into data.

Astronomers must often deal with noisy data. For example, a telescope might measure a tiny dip in a star’s brightness. With such a faint signal, this dip could be noise. However, if a star’s light dims at regular intervals, that could point to a distant planet orbiting that star. The brightness dip would come from the oh-so-slight shadow cast by the planet passing in front of the star. This highlights how understanding noise is crucial to making accurate scientific observations.

In a sentence

Radio data that scientists once misread as “noise” turned out to be real data indicating dense clumps of mysterious intergalactic gas.

title: Analyze This: Color might explain baboon’s link to Egyptian god
excerpt: Ancient Egyptians might have linked hamadryas baboons with the moon god Thoth due to their silvery fur.
content:
One monkey’s moonlike color might explain its link to an ancient Egyptian god.

In ancient Egypt, Thoth was the god of wisdom, magic and the moon. He took two animal forms. One was a black-and-white bird called the African sacred ibis. The other was the silvery hamadryas baboon. But why ancient Egyptians chose these species — especially the baboon — has been a bit of a mystery.

A new study has now revealed that the color of hamadryas baboon fur closely matches that of the moon. The striking resemblance could explain why these monkeys were chosen to embody a lunar deity, the researchers say. They shared their findings in Time and Mind on July 14.

It’s cool to see someone use physics to investigate this historical question, says Julien Cooper. He’s an Egyptologist at Macquarie University in Australia who did not take part in the work. “If we pay close attention to animal characteristics and behavior … we may explain many [still] mysterious aspects of ancient Egyptian religion and magic.”

A curious choice

Nathaniel Dominy got curious about the “baboonification” of Thoth while studying primates in Africa. “There’s just so many puzzling aspects about it,” says Dominy. He’s a primatologist at Dartmouth College in Hanover, N.H.

For one, baboons are not well liked in many parts of Africa, Dominy notes. The monkeys feast on farmers’ crops and sometimes destroy crops without even eating them. “It just drives people bananas,” Dominy says. Why ancient Egyptians chose to represent a god with animals so widely seen today as menaces “boggles the mind.”

Even stranger, baboons are not native to Egypt. Ancient Egyptians imported them as exotic pets. “A lot of gods had animal representations,” such as hippos, crocodiles and falcons, Dominy says. All of those animals lived in ancient Egypt — except the baboon.

To top it off, skeletons and mummified remains of two baboon species have turned up in Egyptian temples and tombs: hamadryas and olive baboons. Yet Thoth only took the form of a hamadryas baboon. That all made Dominy wonder what made this species so special.

Inspiration struck a couple of years ago when Cooper looked into the origin of Thoth’s name. He traced it to an Egyptian root that meant “bright” and “white” — words describing moonlight. This hinted that the ibis might have been picked for such a god because of its bright white feathers.

Dominy and fellow primatologist Cat Hobaiter set out to see if color might likewise link baboons to Thoth. Hobaiter works at the University of St Andrews in Scotland.

Measuring color

Comparing moon and baboon hues was easier said than done. “The problem with colors is that everyone has a different kind of perspective of color,” Dominy says. “The words I use to describe colors may be very different than the words you use.”

To get around that problem, the team used a tool called a spectrometer. The researchers measured how much light of different wavelengths — or colors — reflected off the moon and baboon fur. This set of wavelength data is called a spectral profile. It gives an “unbiased, totally objective” read on an object’s overall color, Dominy explains.

Dominy took a spectrometer to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City. There, he measured the wavelengths of light that bounced off hairs from a dozen olive and hamadryas baboon specimens in the museum’s collection. The spectral profile of the hamadryas species looked just like that of moonlight.

“I almost cried a little bit! It was just so perfect. It was really a satisfying result,” Dominy says. “The spectral profile is really flat between certain wavelengths. And that flatness is what we perceive as silver or white.”

What’s more, the spectral profile of hamadryas baboons was about 65 percent brighter than that of olive baboons. In fact, the especially bright silver-white of hairs on male hamadryas baboons’ cheeks and chests is “brighter than all of the other monkeys that the Egyptians might have known about,” Dominy says. That boosts his and Hobaiter’s suspicion that hamadryas baboons embodied Thoth because they reminded ancient Egyptians of moonlight.

“In this research, we can ‘join the dots,’ so to speak, and get a glimpse into how Egyptians … used their environment to build their pantheon,” Cooper says. (A pantheon is the set of gods in a culture’s mythology.)

Of course, “we can never actually know what people thought” thousands of years ago, Dominy cautions. “But it sure is fun to think about.”

Data Dive

1. What range of wavelengths did the team measure for moonlight and baboon fur?

2. Search the internet to find the range of wavelengths that human eyes can see. How does this compare to the wavelengths measured?

3. At what wavelengths does the moon reflect the most light? What about P. hamadryas baboons? What about P. anubis baboons?

4. Which baboon species reflects more light overall?

5. Which species’ overall pattern of reflected light more closely matches moonlight?

title: Seals long ago evolved to hear above the water — and below
excerpt: Spongy tissue that fills with blood makes this possible, show X-ray scans of hundreds of ears from seals and other animals.
content:
On land, a mother seal can pick out her pup’s cry on a noisy beach. Underwater, seals listen for songs of potential mates or calls warning of predators. This ability to hear well both in and out of the water is unique among mammals. And some marine mammals evolved it nearly 26.7 million years ago, a new study finds.

Seals, sea lions and walruses are known as pinnipeds. They have amphibious hearing — or ears adapted to work well on land and in water. This is “something of a superpower,” says paleontologist James Rule. “They are the only mammals which can do this.” Rule works at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia.

The human ear has an inner chamber filled with air. It conducts sound well when we’re on land but not when we’re underwater. “Water is over 800 times more dense than air,” Rule points out. So sound waves don’t travel to our ears as effectively as they would in air. In fact, less than one percent of underwater sound gets through, he says.

Pinnipeds have spongy tissue inside their ears. It fills with blood when they dive into water. That helps to keep the pressure the same inside and outside their ears. Blood’s density is much closer to that of water. So sound waves moving through water can travel well through that blood, too.

This allows the creatures to hear sounds clearly underwater. They also can filter out background noise. It allows them to better hear useful sounds, Rule says, and to tell what direction they come from.

Swimmers’ ears

It wasn’t clear how pinnipeds developed that trait. So Rule’s team used X-rays to scan 217 ear specimens from museums around the world. The samples included 119 mammal species.

Known as micro-CTs, these scans provided detailed 3-D images of the animals’ ears. It’s “like the scan you would get at the doctor, but much more powerful,” Rule explains — “and for very small objects.”

The scans included specimens from all 34 modern pinniped species. They also scanned ears of other mammals. These included dogs, weasels, otters, raccoons and fossils of their extinct relatives. Among those early ancestors was a creature called Puijila. It spent a lot of time in water but could hear only in air. They also studied animals known as Enaliarctos. Scientists think these were the first fully sea-dwelling pinnipeds.

The team created a family tree of these ancient creatures. Then they looked at how their ears changed over time.

That revealed when animals developed this special tissue that can be filled with blood. And that allowed the researchers to work out when pinnipeds evolved amphibious hearing. The researchers shared their findings July 15 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

Steven Benjamins was surprised at how early underwater hearing emerged. Though not involved in the new study, he is a marine ecologist. He works at the Scottish Association for Marine Science in Oban.

That underwater hearing developed early — in pinniped ancestors — suggests this trait likely aids the animals’ survival. Some of the oldest fossils scanned had ears more like those of otters, Benjamins says. These creatures had lived in shallow waters where underwater hearing wasn’t essential.

Accurate underwater hearing likely became key, he says, as pinnipeds moved into deeper seas.

The ability of the blood-filled tissue to conduct sound began as an accident, the new data suggest. At first, it likely made underwater sounds too loud. But pinniped ears evolved again to adjust to that sound level.

This means they are also incredibly sensitive to sounds, including noise pollution, notes Rule. These animals rely on sound to communicate. Loud sounds, such as from boats, can alter pinniped behaviors, including how they care for their young.

This unique hearing has also endowed many pinnipeds with great rhythm. Like parrots, they can mimic speaking and singing. Says Rule, “The evolution of amphibious hearing has made pinnipeds the masters of sound.”

title: This teen piloted an underwater robot to study kelp forests
excerpt: His observations offer new insight into why some kelp beds are thriving as others are declining.
content:
Linden Hunter-Pinsky, 14, lives by the ocean in Santa Cruz, Calif. There, he sees kelp beds off the coast on his way to school. California’s kelp severely declined in the 2010s due to a heat wave and other factors, Linden recently learned. But some of them near Santa Cruz have begun to bounce back. That made him wonder: Was that because the recovering beds had fewer sea urchins, which graze on kelp?

To find out, Linden looked at satellite data from a site called Kelpwatch. It helped him choose two declining, two recovering and two stable kelp beds in Santa Cruz. He then borrowed a remotely operated vehicle, or ROV, from a local nonprofit. At each kelp bed, he used a remote control to collect video as he steered the ROV underwater.

No kelp bed had many sea urchins, the footage showed. These data hint that sea urchins are likely not why only some kelp beds were recovering. Other factors, such as runoff, likely play a bigger role, Linden suspects.

Kelp ecosystems are home to many species, including endangered ones. Kelp forests also protect shores from erosion and trap climate-warming carbon. So learning what allows kelp to thrive is important.

Linden did his research as a seventh grader at Gateway Middle School in Santa Cruz. His research earned him a finalist spot in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. This program is run by Society for Science, which also publishes Science News Explores. Here, Linden shares his science fair experiences and advice.

What was the biggest challenge of this project?

“Getting to the kelp beds,” Linden says. He couldn’t take a motorboat, because its motor could get caught in the kelp. Instead, he and his dad took out his family’s rowboat, which slowed down travel time to the kelp beds. “I was being jostled around by the waves while staring at this [ROV] controller, and I got seasick,” he says.

What was the most rewarding part?

Seasickness aside, Linden says he enjoyed seeing the kelp forests from the ROV’s point of view. “I had so much fun seeing this fish swim by and another fish swim by,” he says. “I had a lot of fun just seeing the marine life down there that I never see.”

What’s next for you?

“I would love to look more into other factors that might be preventing kelp forest recovery in certain places,” Linden says. He is thinking about ways to extend the project to the kelp forests of Chile, where he is currently living abroad for a year.

Any advice for research newbies?

“Don’t feel constrained by what you think is a good project,” Linden says. “I’d seen so many people with AI [projects], so I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, is my project not good enough?’” What matters most is whether you like your project, Linden says, and whether you want to spend time on it.

title: Canyon Creatures
excerpt: From a research ship off the coast of Argentina, Daniel Lauretta watched a robot sink into the ocean. The robot was named SuBastian. It was a remotely operated vehicle.
content:
From a research ship off the coast of Argentina, Daniel Lauretta watched a robot sink into the ocean. The robot was named SuBastian. It was a remotely operated vehicle. SuBastian was carrying cameras to the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean’s Mar del Plata Canyon. The underwater valley is more than twice as deep as the Grand Canyon. When SuBastian got to the seafloor, Lauretta worried.

“The first thing I saw, once the cameras reached the bottom, was just soft sediment,” he told TIME for Kids. “There were very few animals.” There was no need to worry. Over 21 days in summer 2025, SuBastian dove 17 times. It found coral reefs. It found sea stars. It found animals no person had ever seen. About a year later, a team of scientists examined the mission’s findings.

In September, the team announced that it identified 57 never-seen marine species. Live From the Deep Lauretta is a researcher at the Argentine Museum of Natural Sciences. That’s in Buenos Aires. He led the expedition’s science team, which was run by the Schmidt Ocean Institute. As Lauretta watched SuBastian explore, the cameras streamed live video online. Millions of people tuned in.

Suddenly, an orange sea star came into view. Viewers thought it looked like a character from SpongeBob SquarePants. “The chat exploded with comments about its resemblance to Patrick Star,” Lauretta says. The sea star became famous. It was not a new species. The scientists left it where it was. But the team collected other animals from the canyon and took them to the lab.

That’s where the real discoveries began. Species Detectives In July 2026, 20 taxonomists and other researchers gathered in Buenos Aires for two weeks to study the animals from the canyon. They would figure out which ones were new to science. “It’s like being a detective,” says Francisco Solís-Marín. He’s a sea cucumber expert. To learn whether an animal is a new discovery, he compares its shape and body parts to those of every known species.

One newly discovered sea cucumber is about four inches long. It’s almost transparent. It has bumps that look like horns. The team called it Loki. ”). “Sea cucumbers are some of the ocean’s little superheroes,” Solís-Marín says. “Some can swim, glow, or defend themselves in amazing ways.” The smallest discoveries came from mud: Copepods are crustaceans. They’re smaller than a grain of rice.

Scientists examined only a 10th of the copepod samples. Each was a new species. “There is still a whole new world to discover,” says Emanuel Pereira, a copepod scientist. Lauretta’s team is heading back in early 2027. They’ll explore a different canyon. “I hope to find many new species,” he says. What’s in a Name? Loki is a nickname. But every newly discovered species needs an official scientific name.

To choose it, scientists write a report. They describe how the animal is different from known species. It can take months or years to complete this process. But there’s a reward: “As the scientists studying this new species, we get to choose its official name,” Solís-Marín says. Until then, Loki officially goes by Peniagone sp. The sp. means the species hasn’t yet been named.

title: Analyze This: Microbes can make valuable chemicals more sustainably
excerpt: Food waste-fed bacteria may someday make chemical ingredients for medicines, cosmetics and more.
content:
The secret to making some household products more eco-friendly may lurk in our own guts.

Many medicines, cosmetics and cleaning products are made with medium-chain carboxylic acids, or MCCAs. These chemical ingredients usually come from palm and coconut oil. But growing those crops has downsides for the environment. It often requires chopping down trees to clear land for farming. That destroys the homes of many wildlife species, leading to biodiversity loss.

Scientists Say: Biodiversity

“The major problem right now is how unsustainable the production of these chemicals are,” says Ian Gois. He’s a microbiologist at the University of Toronto in Canada. But some bacteria that dwell in the guts of humans and other animals produce MCCAs, Gois notes. They could be harnessed to make these chemicals in a greener way.

One group of handy microbes are chain-elongating bacteria. These microbes can munch on small molecules and spit out bigger ones. But they don’t always spit out compounds big enough to be MCCAs. Those molecules all feature strings of six to eight carbon atoms.

The compounds that the bacteria pump out depend on what foods the microbes consume. And the ratio, or relative amounts, of different foods can impact the lengths of the molecules they create, Gois says. The exact conditions to coax bacteria into making MCCA-length molecules haven’t been clear.

Gois’ team set out to investigate this. They fed microbes different ratios of foods. Then, they tracked what molecules the microbes made. The two foods the team focused on were acetate and lactate. These small molecules form when organic, or carbon-based, materials break down. They can come from plant or animal matter that gets tossed in the trash.

Scientists Say: Organic

With lower amounts of acetate, some bacteria made longer molecules, including MCCAs. The team watched how the process played out in cells. They made some acetate with carbon atoms that are heavier than usual. That allowed them to track where the acetate went. It showed that one type of chain-elongating bacteria grabbed less acetate from the environment. This microbe could use lactate to make acetate, Gois says. When it did, this microbe made more MCCAs.

The scientists shared their findings in the June issue of Nature Microbiology.

This knowledge could help people put chain-elongating bacteria to work, Gois says. It could also help engineers tweak the genes of microbes to make them even better at making useful molecules.

Explainer: Where fossil fuels come from

In this study, the researchers fed their bacteria specific amounts of certain molecules. But others on Gois’ team are now studying how microbes could make valuable chemicals from food waste. These waste-fed microbes might not only be able to make MCCAs typically drawn from palm and coconut oil. They might also be used to make chemicals that normally come from fossil fuels, Gois says. That could help reduce the use of fossil fuels that contribute to climate change.

Microbes are “cool and versatile,” Gois says — and we’re going to need them as our allies in dealing with climate change.

Busy bacteria

Pseudoramibacter alactolyticus bacteria can use small molecules — such as acetate and lactate — to make larger molecules. Butyrate has four carbons. Hexanoate has six. Octanoate has eight. That makes hexanoate and octanoate MCCAs, which are valuable ingredients for making household products. Researchers fed P. alactolyticus different amounts of acetate and lactate. On the graph, the lowest amount of acetate is on the left and increases along the x-axis. The y-axis shows the concentration of carbon contributed by each compound produced by bacteria (in millimoles of carbon).

Data Dive:

1. At what acetate-to-lactate ratio is the most hexanoate made?

2. As the ratio increases, what happens to the concentration of butyrate?

3. As the ratio increases, what happens to the concentration of octanoate?

4. If researchers wanted to get the most octanoate and hexanoate, what ratio of microbe foods should they use?

title: Some video games offer mental-health benefits
excerpt: The PlaySmart video game lowered teens’ symptoms of depression. This benefit was still there a year after they stopped playing the game.
content:
Playing some video games can be healthy, a new study finds — if they are designed to support mental well-being.

Consider this scenario in PlaySmart. “Taylor was one of my best friends. We drifted away and it feels like it was my fault.”

As you play this game as Taylor’s friend, you see what pushed her away. Then you try making different choices. Along the way, you learn when and how to get Taylor some help. And as you do, the story changes. You two end up staying friends.

This game aims to give teens the tools and confidence to navigate thorny situations involving mental-health struggles or abuse of opioid drugs. Players “see what happens — the good and the bad,” says Lynn Fiellin. A doctor and behavioral scientist, Fiellin works at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth, in Hanover, N.H.

The game was developed, she says, in hopes of lowering a teen’s risk of drug addiction or suffering a real mental-health crisis.

But can a video game really do that?

Fiellin was part of a team that put PlaySmart (and other video games) to the test with human volunteers. And they did it in much the same way scientists check whether medicines or other treatments work. PlaySmart indeed helps boost teens’ mental health, the results now suggest.

These researchers shared their findings August 17 in JAMA Network Open.

Serious fun

Teens who played PlaySmart had fewer depression symptoms a full year later than teens who played a different video game during the trial. “That’s very promising,” says Linda Charmaraman. She directs the Youth, Media & Wellbeing research lab at Wellesley College in Massachusetts. She did not help develop the game.

Many researchers are working on what they call “serious” video games, or ones that benefit society, Charmaraman says. But it’s rare, she notes, for this type of intervention to show an effect that lasts a year or more.

For the trial, Fiellin’s group brought games (and snacks — lots of snacks) to 15 high schools around Connecticut. Students were randomly assigned to either play PlaySmart or to choose a different game. The other games (such as The Sims) hadn’t been designed to teach healthy skills. All recruits played once or twice a week for six weeks.

By the end, kids who’d played PlaySmart knew more about opioid drugs and saw them as more dangerous than those who had played other games. That’s one thing Fiellin says her group had hoped to see. After all, you’re less likely to try something that you see as dangerous. Three months later, the health-gaming group remembered a lot of facts they had learned. But their sense of danger from opioids was fading.

The PlaySmart group’s views on getting help from a therapist or counselor didn’t fade, though. They were more likely to view seeking help as a good thing than were teens who had played another game. And this effect stayed fairly constant throughout the study. This might help explain how playing this game could have reduced teens’ symptoms of depression, the researchers think.

Says Fiellin, just knowing that there are “opportunities and options for help” may have made a difference.

Adds Charmaraman, knowing how and when to seek help is hugely important in depression intervention and prevention. A lot of teens, she says, “feel like they need to wait for something very extreme to happen.” But that’s not true. It’s better to ask for help early than wait for a crisis, she explains.

For kids already interested in gaming, she thinks it makes sense to choose a game that could boost social skills and mental health.

Meeting teens where they are

PlaySmart is one of five games, and counting, created by the play2PREVENT Lab. Fiellin launched this lab in 2009 after noticing how engrossed her own kids were in gaming. “I thought this was a way we could deliver healthy information and skill-building to kids,” she recalls.

She wanted to meet kids where they already are — on screens.

Caroline Barry, a behavioral health scientist, joined the lab because she was excited about leveraging screen time for good. Depression, anxiety, addiction and other issues are widespread among today’s teens, she notes. Traditional prevention strategies rely mainly on in-person programs at schools and community centers. Putting the same kind of teaching into games, Barry says, could “have more reach and potentially broader impact.”

She, Fiellin and other experts in health and education teamed up with video-game designers to make each game. They also have been inviting teens to give feedback on early versions of each. In the past, Fiellin points out, these teen critics have said things like, “No one would ever wear that.” They’ve also pointed out when the slang being used was out of date.

When each game is ready, the company Playbl helps get it into the hands of teens. They don’t post the games on app stores. Instead, teachers or school administrators can reach out to get a program started at their school.

PlaySmart is a relatively new game. Another one, Smokescreen, focuses on preventing kids from vaping and smoking. It has almost 10,000 active players right now, says Kirby Salerno, who runs Playbl.

What’s next? Fiellin’s team is now working on two new games. One is for kids with autism and their families. It focuses on identifying strengths of neurodivergent people. Another game will focus on social media and mental health.

“The idea,” says Fiellin, “will be to help kids and their parents know how to navigate social media and make better choices.”

title: Four T. rex footprints hint at how fast it traveled
excerpt: Though poorly preserved, the prints suggest the dino ambled at 1.6 meters per second, roughly the speed of a human walking briskly.
content:
Four fossilized footprints are helping scientists step into a dinosaur’s shoes. The prints form the first known set of tracks likely left by an adult Tyrannosaurus rex.

A trackway is three or more consecutive footprints left by some animal. The one for this T. rex spans 7 meters (10 feet). The track spacing suggests the ancient predator had been ambling along at about 1.6 meters (5.2 feet) per second, which would be a quick walking pace for us.

A few single adult T. rex footprints have been recorded. So have trackways from what might be T. rex juveniles or another related species, says Peter Falkingham. He’s a paleontologist at Liverpool John Moores University in England.

Let’s learn about trace fossils

“Finding an adult trackway is cool,” he says. “It’s unique. It brings something new.”

The reason: “An individual [footprint] doesn’t tell you a lot,” Falkingham explains. “A trackway tells you more about foot placement as the animal’s moving along.” And younger and older dinosaurs likely walked differently, just as human toddlers and adults do.

Kent Hups teaches at Northglenn High School, outside Denver, Colo. (A paleontologist, he also works at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.) Hups stumbled on the trackway while fossil hunting in North Dakota last year. It stuck up out of the ground along a steep incline in the Hell Creek Formation. Sediment had filled in the originally muddy footprints and fossilized. It then eroded away more slowly than the surrounding rock.

The first print that he found was three-toed and enormous. It measured 80 centimeters (31.5 inches) across. He recalls immediately thinking: “This has to be a T. rex.”

Slender toe impressions and fossils unearthed in the area signal the trackway had been left behind roughly 66.5 million years ago. “There’s always the possibility that we haven’t found the skeletons of some species that we don’t know about,” Falkingham says. “But as far as our knowledge goes, T. rex is about the only track-maker that could have made these.”

He and Hups were part of a team that used stride length and body size to gauge the dinosaur’s speed. Unfortunately, the footprints aren’t well-preserved. And estimating speed from tracks is tricky. So the T. rex may have been walking slightly faster or slower than what they reported September 8 in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

Better tracks could have revealed whether the foot landed flat or toe-to-heel — or even how its foot pads supported the dino’s weight.

More tracks are sure to follow. In fact, a fifth step may be concealed in the hill. But the team is waiting for Mother Nature to wear away the surrounding rock, Hups says. “I can’t wait to get back out there and keep looking for more.”

title: Meet Swiftiephylus, a group of insects named after Taylor Swift
excerpt: Four newly described species of Australian plant bug have been named in honor of world-famous pop star Taylor Swift.
content:
Blonde with a pop of red? Could be the superstar singer Taylor Swift. Or maybe a true bug named for her.

Scientists named the tiny, big-eyed Australian bugs to honor record-breaking, world-famous music icon Taylor Swift. This Swiftiephylus group recognizes her “show-stopping talent, heart-wrenching lyrics, and the joy and comfort she has brought to many.” That’s what researchers wrote when they described the insects September 9 in Insect Systematics & Evolution.

Explainer: Insects, arachnids and other arthropods

There are some 10,000 species of plant bugs found all over the world. Like their name suggests, they’re plant-munchers. But little had been known about their diversity in Australia.

Insect biologist Christiane Weirauch works at the University of California, Riverside. In 2022, another entomologist, Sarah Schroeder, began her PhD work with Weirauch. Some of these mystery bugs became a part of her research.

“I was really excited,” Schroeder says. “It’s a dream thing for a scientist to get to describe new species.”

Little insects, big honor

Schroeder and Weirauch studied flower-eating plant bugs found in Australia’s she-oak trees. Each bug is about the size of a head of a pin. By comparing their body shapes, colors and genes to those of known species, the researchers found 12 new species. They organized them into five groups, each containing closely related species. Each group is known as a genus. One genus — Swiftiephylus — bears a name with special meaning to Schroeder.

“I’ve been a lifelong Swiftie,” Schroeder says. “Taylor’s music has underscored so many of the major milestones of my life. So it felt authentic to me to honor her by naming these species after her and giving her a gift back for all of her music.”

Schroeder picked the four species to bear Swift’s name because of their yellow colors accented with splashes of red. “Taylor’s pretty well known for having her red lip,” Schroeder says. “And the fans affectionately call her Blondie.”

Beyond the obviously named S. taylorae, Schroeder gave the other three species Latin translations of some of Swift’s album names. S. amator is for Lover. S. intrepidus is for Fearless. And S. poetorum references The Tortured Poet’s Department.

For Schroeder, this song isn’t finished. Swiftiephylus barely scratches the surface of unknown insect life. She notes that it’s crucial to describe species in order to conserve them. You can’t protect what you don’t know is there, she explains. With possibly millions of undescribed insect species still out there, it’s a conservation problem researchers know “All Too Well.”

title: Star Power: Olivia Ryerson
excerpt: Meet Service Star Olivia Ryerson, 14. A nationally ranked chess player, Olivia runs a free girls’ chess club at her high school, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
content:
Meet Service Star Olivia Ryerson, 14. A nationally ranked chess player, Olivia runs a free girls’ chess club at her high school, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Olivia also runs chess tournaments and donates the proceeds to breast cancer research. (And she’s a TFK Kid Reporter alumna!) TFK reader Lassya Fenning spoke with Olivia about her ongoing efforts. How do you get girls plugged into chess?

At my school, I manage an all-girls chess club where girls learn, play, and improve together. Girls make up only about 10% of tournament chess players, so my school’s Queens Club provides a community for them to develop skills. I also run a Philadelphia-based chess tutoring service for girls. S. Chess Federation tournament director. Creating a community of girls who love the game is incredibly important.

What do you enjoy about volunteering? Seeing other girls fall in love with chess is rewarding. I want girls to have the opportunities I’ve had and to share my passion for the game. What challenges have you faced? One of the biggest challenges is building a sustainable community that keeps people coming back. Also, interested girls come from many different schools and areas in Philadelphia, so logistical planning and outreach are difficult.

I’m still learning, but the rewards make it worth it. You donated funds from your chess tournaments to raise money for breast cancer research. What inspired you to do this? I’ve researched the side effects of medications used to keep breast cancer in remission—specifically how they can reduce cognitive skills and quality of life. Since chess is shown to increase cognitive function and focus, I chose to support a group called Living Beyond Breast Cancer.

It works to improve the quality of life for patients. I hope to help that mission while building a community of chess players who care. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

title: A World Without Imagination
excerpt: TFK Kid Reporter Adam Sadi read Building 903 and interviewed its author, Lois Lowry. Lowry also wrote The Giver, a 1993 Newbery Medal–winning dystopian novel. Read Adam’s thoughts below.
content:
TFK Kid Reporter Adam Sadi read Building 903 and interviewed its author, Lois Lowry. Lowry also wrote The Giver, a 1993 Newbery Medal–winning dystopian novel. Read Adam’s thoughts below. It’s 2099, and the world is totally different: only one country, one dictator, and zero books. And there’s no imagination—because it’s forbidden! That’s life for 14-year-old twins Tessa and Theo in Lois Lowry’s new book, Building 903.

When Theo disappears, Tessa and her parents search for him. And in solving the mystery, they uncover things that their society has kept hidden. An elderly neighbor gives Tessa a key that leads to a secret stash of books. Tessa has never read or even held a book before. These unfamiliar objects hold clues to Theo’s disappearance. As Tessa discovers what stories can do, she begins to understand what people lose when they’re not allowed to read.

Building 903 is about what happens when people lose their imagination. Lowry told TFK that imagination helps us put ourselves into “the mind, the soul, the heart of another human being.” When she writes, she imagines what her characters think and feel. In real life, this same skill—empathy—helps us understand other people. Lowry leaves some work for her readers, too.

“I did leave some things unanswered, and I did that on purpose,” she says. These mysteries give kids something to discuss, and a reason to use their own imagination. Building 903 made me think about the future. Its dystopian world is scary, but the book also left me thinking about hope. If stories and imagination help us understand one another, maybe they can help us have more empathy and make better choices, too. I recommend this book to readers who enjoy mysteries and stories about different worlds and big questions.

title: Scientists Say: Abyssal Zone
excerpt: This layer of the ocean lies far out of reach of sunlight. Yet, life still thrives.
content:
Abyssal Zone, (noun, “ab-IZ-sell ZONE”)

The abyssal zone is the second-deepest zone of the ocean.

Scientists describe the ocean’s depths in five layers. The abyssal zone is the fourth layer. The abyssal zone includes both the water itself and the seafloor. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, says this zone begins at a depth of 4,000 meters (13,100 feet). Other experts say it starts at a depth of 2,000 meters (6,600 feet). Everyone agrees, however, that it extends to a depth of 6,000 meters (19,700 feet).

Light usually shines through the ocean’s top layer. That’s why scientists call this layer the sunlight zone. The sunlight zone ends at a depth of 200 meters (660 feet). That’s where the twilight zone begins. As you descend through the twilight zone, sunlight fades. By the time you reach the third layer — the midnight zone — all surface light is gone. This layer begins at a depth of 1,000 meters (3,300 feet). Descending below the midnight zone brings you to the abyssal zone. Below the abyssal zone lies the hadal zone.

The abyssal zone is cold, dark and under massive pressure from the water above. Temperatures remain near-freezing. Sunlight never penetrates to these depths. The only light there comes from life forms. Some living things here are bioluminescent. That means they produce light. These species often use that light to draw in prey or mates.

Animals and microbes live in the abyssal zone. One type of life you will not find there, however, is plants. They get their energy through photosynthesis, which relies on sunlight. In the sunless abyssal zone, they could not survive.

With no plants to support the food chain directly, life in the abyssal zone must rely on other food sources. Organic material drifts down from the surface. Microbes or animals may eat that material. That organic material may be tiny particles. Or it could be the body of a dead whale. Chemicals arising from deep below the Earth — such as from hydrothermal vents — may also support deep sea life.

Only a few parts of Earth’s oceans go deep enough to include all five ocean layers. The Mariana Trench is one example. This deep ocean trench lies in the Western Pacific Ocean. It descends to a depth of almost 11,000 meters (36,000 feet). Descending into this trench would take you through all five major zones of the ocean, including the abyssal zone.

title: TFK at New York Comic Con
excerpt: TFK Kid Reporter Shaiyar Dhillon attended New York Comic Con in October. In this article, he shares his experience with TIME for Kids readers.
content:
TFK Kid Reporter Shaiyar Dhillon attended New York Comic Con in October. In this article, he shares his experience with TIME for Kids readers. Every year since 2006, thousands gather at New York City’s Javits Center to take part in one of the world’s largest comic and pop culture events. My family and I have been going to New York Comic Con (NYCC) since I was about seven months old: I wore a Superman onesie.

We love to read comics and books, cosplay, and watch our favorite superhero shows and movies. For us, NYCC is an annual family celebration. Over the years, I’ve cosplayed some of my favorite characters, such as Dipper from Gravity Falls, Hunter from The Owl House, and Miles Morales from Spider-Man. I’ve also cosplayed Percy Jackson from Rick Riordan’s best-selling Percy Jackson series.

At this year’s NYCC, I got to meet Riordan, and other authors, as well. Authors Abound Randy Ribay is a National Book Award finalist who writes the Avatar: Last Airbender books. When I met him, Ribay told me he got the gig because he was both a writer and a fan. In 2020, he watched the whole series on Netflix and “did one of those long Twitter threads where I watched an episode and then would type up my reactions, my analysis of the episode.

And I did that for the entire series. Somebody [saw] that at some point, and they’re like, ‘Oh yeah, this writer is a fan. Let’s ask him.’” Pretty cool. Next up from Ribay is his third Avatar book, about Avatar Sonam. The book was announced at Comic Con. My family and I spent some time strolling through NYCC’s Artist Alley.

I got to meet Kami Garcia, who writes the Teen Titans series. I also met Zeno Robinson, who voices Goh in Pokémon Journeys and Hunter in The Owl House. He signed my Owl House graphic novel. On Sunday, the last day of Comic Con, I spoke with one of my favorite writers, Rick Riordan. You know him as the creator of the Percy Jackson universe.

Riordan was at Comic Con to chat about his new book, The Wild Zone, which came out in September. It’s the first book of the Camp Half-Blood Chronicles. Riordan was joined on a panel by series coauthors Annabelle Oh, Kyle Lukoff, Pablo Cartaya, and Jade Adia. Oh cowrote the first book in the series. During the panel, she said that main character Katie Kim is “a daughter of Aries, and she’s an underwhelming daughter of Aries.

.  She’s kind of in everyone’s shadow.” Oh added that Katie is “trying to make her way and prove herself”—just like most of us. Time to Chat After the panel, I got to sit down with Riordan and Oh and ask them questions about Camp Half-Blood: The Wild Zone. Here’s part of our conversation. Shaiyar: Can you tell me about the origins of the Camp Half-Blood series, and how you met the collaborators?

Riordan: I was on set with the Percy Jackson TV show, and we were having conversations about what we could do with the sets between seasons. That got me thinking about if there were stories that we could tell that happened between The Lightning Thief and The Sea of Monsters. I started brainstorming, and I came up with this idea: What if we had four new heroes?

And what if I could find four great other authors who could each take one of their voices and bring them to life? Shaiyar: How does it feel to write in a universe like Percy Jackson? Were you a fan? Oh: I was. I read them a long time ago, when the first book came out. Rick has such a conversational and approachable voice for readers.

It’s like you’re hanging out with a friend and the friend is just telling you a fun story. So I liked his writing style, and I enjoyed his books. When I got the opportunity to work on this, it was an honor. But it was also intimidating, because I know how beloved that world and those characters are. I had to make sure I worked very, very hard to do all of my research on the past material and to make sure I knew enough about the world that I would not let the fans down.

Shaiyar: What do you like better, working on TV or writing books? Riordan: Writing books. I mean, that’s where I live. No offense to the television industry: They do amazing work. But it’s not my world. I’m lucky that they invited me in and I got to learn more about it. But I am first and foremost always a novelist.

Shaiyar: Is there a scoop you can give us about Season 3 of the show? Riordan: All I can tell you is that I think it’s the best one yet. You should totally watch it. I think you’ll like it! This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
